evidence.claim: SR 89A traverses the Prescott National Forest at Mingus Mountain in Arizona’s Black Hills.
evidence.quote: Mingus Mountain (Yavapai: Hwa:lkyañaña) is a mountain located in the U.S. state of Arizona in the Black Hills mountain range. It is located within the Prescott National Forest traversed by State Route 89A

evidence.claim: Forest Service roads branch from the highway toward the summit, where views include the Verde Valley and Sycamore Canyon Wilderness.
evidence.quote: The summit can be reached via Forest Service roads that branch off from State Route 89A. From the mountain, there are views of the Verde Valley, Sycamore Canyon Wilderness

evidence.claim: The Forest Service describes a pine setting with hiking, camping, hang gliding and paragliding.
evidence.quote: Located in the cool pines of central Arizona, Mingus Mountain offers a wide range of recreational opportunities including picnicking, hiking, horseback riding, mountain biking, camping, fishing, hunting, hang gliding, and paragliding.

evidence.claim: Jerome’s mining industry built its own transport connections: United Verde constructed wagon roads to Prescott, the Verde Valley and the railroad depot at Ash Fork.
evidence.quote: United Verde built a small smelter at Jerome and constructed wagon roads from it to Prescott, the Verde Valley, and the Atlantic and Pacific Railroad depot at Ash Fork.

evidence.claim: Wagon transport proved expensive, and the company stopped operations in late 1884 after copper prices fell.
evidence.quote: However, transport by wagon was expensive, and in late 1884 after the price of copper had fallen by 50%, the company ceased all operations at the site.

evidence.claim: William A. Clark bought the properties four years later and ordered a narrow-gauge railway to Jerome Junction.
evidence.quote: He ordered construction of a narrow-gauge railway, the United Verde and Pacific, to Jerome Junction

evidence.claim: Coming from the Prescott side, the mountain excursion branches off SR 89A before the journey reaches Jerome.
evidence.quote: The summit can be reached via Forest Service roads that branch off from State Route 89A.

evidence.claim: Woodchute Wilderness lies north of the highway’s highest point.
evidence.quote: The Woodchute Wilderness, north of the highest point of 89A

evidence.claim: Jerome occupies Cleopatra Hill above the Verde Valley, its surviving buildings set along winding roads on the steep mountainside.
evidence.quote: The community retains much of the look and feel of an early 20th-century mining town, with buildings perched along the winding roads of the steeply sloped mountainside.

evidence.claim: William A. Clark bought the properties four years later
evidence.quote: Four years later, William A. Clark, who had made a fortune in mining and commercial ventures in Montana, bought the United Verde properties

evidence.claim: A 60-foot steel fire tower stands atop Mingus Mountain, replacing a shorter wooden tower in 1935.
evidence.quote: The fire tower is a 60 feet (18 m) Pacific Coast Steel tower built in 1935.  It replaced a 41 feet (12 m) wooden tower.

evidence.claim: Its wooden cab has an overhanging front porch and a gabled roof.
evidence.quote: The tower has a 7 feet (2.1 m) by 7 feet (2.1 m) wooden cab with an overhanging front porch and a gable roof.

evidence.claim: The lookout complex entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.
evidence.quote: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.

evidence.claim: Forest Service roads reach the summit from SR 89A.
evidence.quote: The summit can be reached via Forest Service roads that branch off from State Route 89A.

evidence.claim: The mountain offers views of the Verde Valley and Sycamore Canyon Wilderness; the surrounding recreation area includes a small lake periodically stocked with rainbow trout.
evidence.quote: A small lake located in the cool pines of Mingus Mountain, Mingus Lake is periodically stocked with rainbow trout.

evidence.claim: Jerome’s buildings follow winding streets on a steep mountainside above the Verde Valley.
evidence.quote: with buildings perched along the winding roads of the steeply sloped mountainside.

evidence.claim: The copper mines supported more than 10,000 residents in the 1920s, but the population fell below 100 after mining ended in 1953.
evidence.quote: Supported in its heyday by rich copper mines, it was home to more than 10,000 people in the 1920s.

evidence.claim: In 1956, the society completed negotiations with Phelps Dodge to prevent further demolition in the town’s main area.
evidence.quote: In 1956 the society completed negotiations with Phelps Dodge assuring that no more buildings would be torn down in the main part of Jerome.

evidence.claim: Houses, commercial buildings and civic buildings survive within the historic district.
evidence.quote: In addition to houses, commercial and civic buildings survive

evidence.claim: the population fell below 100 after mining ended in 1953.
evidence.quote: Mining continued at a reduced level in the Verde District until 1953, when Phelps Dodge shut down the United Verde Mine and related operations. Jerome's population subsequently fell below 100.

evidence.claim: Jerome’s third jail began as part of a larger wood-and-tin structure, built in 1905.
evidence.quote: The building, the city's third jail, was initially a part of a larger structure made from wood and tin. The jail, built in 1905

evidence.claim: In 1938, it began moving downhill after dynamite blasting changed the mountainside.
evidence.quote: began sliding in 1938 when the shape of the mountain it sat on changed after it was blasted with dynamite.

evidence.claim: The jail tore free of the original building and ended up on Hull Avenue.
evidence.quote: tearing away from its original building. When it was finished sliding, the jail ended up directly on Hull Ave.

evidence.claim: Residents changed the road to pass it; Arizona’s transportation department later moved the jail to its present position.
evidence.quote: Instead of removing the jail, citizens altered the road to go around the building. It was eventually moved to its current spot by the Arizona Department of Transportation.

evidence.claim: The Jerome Historical Society took control in 2017 and stabilized the remaining walls.
evidence.quote: In 2017, the Jerome Historical Society gained control of the jail and, to make sure the building did not collapse, stabilized the remaining walls.

evidence.claim: Hang gliding and paragliding are among the Forest Service’s listed activities here, alongside hiking, horseback riding and mountain biking in the pines.
evidence.quote: Mingus Mountain offers a wide range of recreational opportunities including picnicking, hiking, horseback riding, mountain biking, camping, fishing, hunting, hang gliding, and paragliding.

evidence.claim: The town also endured ground subsidence: dozens of buildings, including the post office and jail, were lost as the ground sank during the 1930s.
evidence.quote: Meanwhile, a subsidence problem that had irreparably damaged at least 10 downtown buildings by 1928 worsened through the 1930s. Dozens of buildings, including the post office and jail, were lost as the earth beneath them sank away.

evidence.claim: In 1953, residents organized the Jerome Historical Society and opened a museum.
evidence.quote: They organized the Jerome Historical Society in 1953 and opened a museum and gift shop.

evidence.claim: Earth movement left the structure unusable but did not destroy it completely. An iron fence surrounds the surviving jail, whose walls were stabilized.
evidence.quote: Rendered unusable but not completely destroyed by earth movements since the 1930s

flags: ADOT cache files 00 and 15–17 contain only Wayback headers, not the corridor plan. Cannot verify scenic designation, designation rationale/date, road-building history, exact corridor endpoints or length. Overview uses supported geography and separate mining transport history. The overview is deliberately short because the saved evidence says little about driving the designated road itself.

Dropped current claims about Yaeger Canyon, roadside ponderosa, basalt pockets, narrow canyons, Mogollon Rim views, steep highway descent, two lanes, shoulder absence, guardrails and switchbacks because the plan text is missing. Existing switchbacks motif retained as required; it remains unverified but is not contradicted.

Dropped Spanish claims dated 1582/1598 and Army rediscovery in 1875: not supported by cache. Jerome article instead gives 1585 Spanish observations and 1876 mining claims; neither incidental chronology is reused.
Jerome and its historic-district article disagree on landmark year (1967/1966); year omitted. Sliding distance also differs (about 200/about 225 feet); distance omitted.
No strip towns were supplied. Order follows mountain excursion, Jerome town, then its jail; these are geographic anchors, not verified parking locations.
Lookout designation does not establish tower access; no climbing invitation or opening claim is made. Mountain naming accounts and elevations conflict, so both are omitted.
